authoredSolutions.112: Molarity is moles of solute per LITRE of solution. The beaker is lidded and the solubility is stated to be unchanged, so the number of moles of NaCl in solution is fixed; only the volume changes, and \(M \propto 1/V\). Water has its maximum density (minimum volume) at \(4\,^{\circ}C\). Heating from \(1\,^{\circ}C\) to \(4\,^{\circ}C\) therefore CONTRACTS the solution, so the volume falls and the molarity RISES; above \(4\,^{\circ}C\) the water expands normally, the volume grows and the molarity FALLS. The correct plot rises to a maximum near \(4\,^{\circ}C\) and then decreases steadily up to \(25\,^{\circ}C\).
authoredSolutions.113: For an isothermal expansion the reversible (infinite stage) path keeps the external pressure only infinitesimally below the gas pressure, so it delivers the MAXIMUM work: \(|w_{a}| > |w_{b}|\). For a compression the reversible path keeps the external pressure only infinitesimally above the gas pressure, so it requires the MINIMUM work, and the single stage compression against a large constant pressure requires the most: \(|w_{d}| > |w_{c}|\). Finally, the reversible isothermal work has the same magnitude \(nRT\ln(V_{2}/V_{1})\) whether the gas expands or is compressed, so \(|w_{a}| = |w_{c}|\). Combining: \(d > c = a > b\).
authoredSolutions.114: Three requirements must all be met by the energy profile. (i) \(A \rightarrow B\) is the slow step, so its activation barrier must be the LARGEST of the three humps. (ii) \(\Delta H\) for that step is positive, so the intermediate B must lie ABOVE A. (iii) The next two steps are exothermic and the reaction evolves heat overall, so C lies below B, D lies below C and, crucially, D lies BELOW A. Only the first profile shows a first barrier larger than the two that follow, an intermediate B above A, and a final level D clearly below A. In the other three either the product is drawn at or above the level of A (so the overall reaction would not be exothermic) or the last step carries the tallest barrier, contradicting 'fast'.

The hydrides \(H_{2}O, H_{2}S, H_{2}Se, H_{2}Te\) become progressively more acidic down the group because the E-H bond gets longer and weaker, so \(TeH_{2}\) (\(H_{2}Te\)) is strongly ACIDIC, the most acidic of the group 16 hydrides. Hence oxidising and acidic, respectively.
authoredSolutions.116: (A) The figure shows two molecules of an aryl halide coupling with sodium in dry ether to give biphenyl. Coupling of two ARYL halides by sodium is the Fittig reaction, so (A)-(III). (B) \(ArN_{2}^{+}X^{-}\) treated with a copper(I) halide in the corresponding halogen acid gives \(ArCl\) and nitrogen: this is the Sandmeyer reaction. (C) \(C_{2}H_{5}Br + NaI\) in dry acetone gives \(C_{2}H_{5}I + NaBr\), the halide exchange known as the Finkelstein reaction, so (C)-(II). (D) The figure shows a tertiary alcohol, 2-methylpropan-2-ol, converted to the tertiary chloride by HCl with anhydrous \(ZnCl_{2}\) (Lucas reagent), the Groove's process. Only option (B) is consistent with both firmly identified pairings (A)-(III) and (C)-(II).
authoredSolutions.117: For \(A(g) \rightleftharpoons B(g) + C(g)\) starting from 1 mole of A, the equilibrium mole fractions are \(\frac{1-\alpha}{1+\alpha}, \frac{\alpha}{1+\alpha}, \frac{\alpha}{1+\alpha}\), so \(K_{p} = \frac{\alpha^{2}p}{1-\alpha^{2}}\), which rearranges to \(\alpha = \sqrt{\frac{K_{p}}{K_{p}+p}}\). This is a decreasing function of \(p\): raising the total pressure shifts the equilibrium towards the side with fewer moles of gas (Le Chatelier), so \(\alpha\) DECREASES, making (B) true and (D) false. If \(p \gg K_{p}\) then \(\alpha \rightarrow 0\), not 1, so (A) is false. If \(K_{p} \gg p\) then \(\alpha \rightarrow 1\), i.e. close to unity rather than much less than unity, so (C) is false.
authoredSolutions.118: For Haber's process \(N_{2} + 3H_{2} \rightleftharpoons 2NH_{3}\), \(\Delta H^{o} \approx -92\) kJ/mol and \(\Delta S^{o} \approx -198\) J/K/mol, both NEGATIVE and both essentially independent of temperature, so they must be drawn as horizontal lines below zero (near \(-100\) and \(-200\) on the scale shown). Dividing \(\Delta G^{o} = \Delta H^{o} - T\Delta S^{o}\) by \(-T\) gives \(-\frac{\Delta G^{o}}{T} = \frac{-\Delta H^{o}}{T} + \Delta S^{o}\). Since \(-\Delta H^{o}\) is positive, \(-\Delta H^{o}/T\) is a positive hyperbola that decays towards zero and never crosses the axis, while \(-\Delta G^{o}/T\) starts positive, falls, crosses zero at the temperature where the reaction stops being spontaneous, and tends to \(\Delta S^{o}\). Only the first plot shows all four curves with these signs and shapes.
authoredSolutions.119: The tetrapeptide contains Gly, Ala, Val and Leu in equimolar proportion, i.e. exactly one residue of each. A peptide chain is directional, running from the N-terminal to the C-terminal residue, so every distinct arrangement of the four different residues is a distinct peptide. The number of sequences is the number of permutations of four distinct objects, \(4! = 4 \times 3 \times 2 \times 1 = 24\).

authoredSolutions.121: Read successive half-lives off the decay curve: the concentration is \(40\) g/L at \(t = 5\) s and \(20\) g/L at \(t = 15\) s, a halving in 10 s; it is \(20\) g/L at \(t = 15\) s and \(10\) g/L at \(t = 25\) s, again a halving in 10 s. authoredSolutions.122: A \(0.2\%\) (w/v) solution contains \(0.2\) g NaOH in 100 mL, i.e. \(2\) g/L, so \(c = 2/40 = 0.05\) mol/L \(= 50\) mol \(m^{-3}\). Molar conductivity \(\Lambda_{m} = \kappa/c = 1.1494/50 = 0.02299\ S\,m^{2}\,mol^{-1}\). authoredSolutions.123: 2-Bromopentane, \(C_{5}H_{11}Br\), has molar mass \(5(12) + 11(1) + 80 = 151\) g/mol, so 151 g is exactly 1 mol. Alcoholic KOH causes E2 dehydrohalogenation, and by Saytzeff's rule the more substituted alkene is the major product, so \(P =\) pent-2-ene, formed in \(80\%\) yield \(= 0.8\) mol. Bromine adds across the double bond in \(100\%\) yield to give \(Q = \) 2,3-dibromopentane, \(C_{5}H_{10}Br_{2}\), of molar mass \(60 + 10 + 160 = 230\) g/mol. Mass of Q \(= 0.8 \times 230 = 184\) g.
authoredSolutions.124: Elevation of boiling point: \(\Delta T_{b} = K_{b}m = K_{b}\frac{w/M}{W_{kg}}\). With \(w = 1\) g and \(W = 0.015\) kg, \(\Delta T_{b} = \frac{0.5}{0.015\,M} = \frac{33.33}{M}\). For AB: \(2.7 = 33.33/M_{AB}\), so \(M_{AB} = 12.35\). As a multiple of \(10^{-1}\) this is \(24.7 \approx 25\).
authoredSolutions.125: First find n. \(K_{2}[NiCl_{4}]\): \(Ni^{2+}\) is \(d^{8}\) and chloride is weak field, so the tetrahedral complex has 2 unpaired electrons and is paramagnetic. \([Zn(H_{2}O)_{6}]Cl_{2}\): \(Zn^{2+}\) is \(d^{10}\), diamagnetic. \(K_{3}[Mn(CN)_{6}]\): \(Mn^{3+}\) is \(d^{4}\) and cyanide is strong field, giving \(t_{2g}^{4}\) with 2 unpaired electrons, paramagnetic. \([Cu(PPh_{3})_{3}I]\): copper is \(+1\), \(d^{10}\), diamagnetic. So \(n = 2\). Next, the enthalpy of atomisation is lowest for the metal with the weakest metallic bonding, which is zinc (about 126 kJ/mol against 281 for Mn, 339 for Cu and 430 for Ni) because its \(3d\) subshell is completely filled and contributes nothing to metallic bonding. The ion is therefore \(Zn^{2+}\), a \(d^{10}\) ion with zero unpaired electrons, so \(\mu = \sqrt{0(0+2)} = 0\) BM.
